outcomes.text: Study Vigil (2021) and The Avengers (1966) as a case study of continuity and change in mainstream TV drama.
Apply all four framework areas and the social, cultural and (for The Avengers) historical contexts to each programme.
Analyse an unseen extract from either programme, making judgements and drawing conclusions.
Compare how the two products reflect their different periods, including the genre, serial narrative, channel and regulation context.
Study The Lego Movie as tent-pole film production by a global conglomerate, in terms of media industries only.
Study The Lego Movie posters and UK TV trailer in relation to media language and representations.
Explain how organisations target audiences through marketing and the assumptions they make about them.
Explain how audiences may read the same product very differently because of social and individual differences.
Study The Lego Movie video game through media industries, audiences and language.
Explain vertical integration, cross-platform release and ownership in the making and release of the game.
Explain intertextual links to other Warner Bros franchises and to Lego, and how technology shapes the game.
Explain the forms of media language used to create meaning in media products.
Apply semiotic analysis, including denotation and connotation.
Explain how selection, combination and exclusion of elements shape meaning, narratives, points of view and messages.
Explain how technology and media products relate to each other.
Explain how codes and conventions become established as genres and how they vary over time.
Apply genre theory: repetition and variation, the dynamic nature of genre, hybridity and intertextuality.
Explain how links between different media products influence meaning.
Apply narrative theories, including those from Propp.
Explain how the media re-present the world and construct versions of reality.
Explain the choices producers make about representing events, groups and ideas.
Explain how reality may be represented differently depending on producers' purposes.
Apply theories of representation: selection, construction and mediation.
Explain the functions of stereotypes, how they become established and change, and why audiences use them to read media quickly.
Explain how and why social groups are under-represented or misrepresented.
Apply gender and representation theories, including feminist approaches.
Explain how representations, including self-representations, carry viewpoints, messages, values and beliefs.
Explain the social, cultural and political significance of representations in terms of the issues addressed.
Apply the feminist concept of patriarchy to representations.
Explain how representations reflect the social, historical and cultural contexts of production.
Explain what affects audience interpretation of representations, including their own experiences and beliefs.
Describe media production by large organisations that own their products and by individuals and groups.
Explain how production processes, people and technologies affect the final product, and how products differ by time and place.
Explain conglomerate ownership, diversification and vertical integration and their effects.
Explain the impact of convergence across platforms and national settings.
Compare government-funded, not-for-profit and commercial funding models.
Explain how media work as global commercial industries reaching large and specialised audiences.
Describe the functions and types of media regulation.
Explain the challenges 'new' digital technologies pose for regulation.
Explain how and why products are aimed at small specialised to large mass audiences.
Explain how media organisations categorise audiences.
Explain how organisations target audiences through marketing and the assumptions they make.
Explain the role of technology in reaching and identifying audiences and in how they consume media.
Explain how audiences interpret the same product differently for social and individual reasons.
Apply theories of active and passive audiences, audience response and interpretation.
Explain the social, cultural and political significance of products and the needs and desires they meet.
Explain how media practices connect to identity, including actual and desired self.
Apply Blumler and Katz's Uses and Gratifications theory.
Explain how and why audience responses to products change over time.
Explain how media products reflect the society of their production and target audience.
Explain how media products reflect the arts and popular culture of their time.
Explain how media products reflect historical events and social change.
Explain how media products reflect political viewpoints, messages, values and beliefs.
Study one complete edition of MOJO magazine across all four framework areas and social and cultural contexts.
Analyse two MOJO front covers (image, masthead, main coverline, coverlines, selling lines) for media language and representation.
Explain how ownership, commercial funding, regulation, readership measurement and audience address work for a magazine.
Compare one set pair of music videos for media language, representations and audiences.
Analyse music video elements: locations, costumes, shot, framing, angle, lighting, lip-synching, performance and editing, including montage.
Explain how audiences interpret the same video differently and how media practices link to identity.
Study one complete episode of BBC Radio 1 Live Lounge in terms of media industries and audiences.
Explain Radio 1's public service role within the BBC, its regulation and its distinct mode of address.
Study The Observer's website (home page and one more page) and its X and Instagram feeds across all four framework areas.
Explain how The Observer is owned and funded and how funding pushed it online.
Explain convergence across platforms and regulation challenges for online and social news.
Explain how online audiences are categorised and how the same content reads differently across platforms.
Explain how media language and technology create meaning and re-present the world in online news.
Study three historical (1966 and 1968) and two contemporary Observer front covers for language, representation and context.
Explain how newspaper front covers use language, layout, typography and photo editing to construct representations.
Explain newspaper production, ownership, funding, convergence and regulation, using one complete print edition.
Compare how the 1960s and present-day covers show changing social, cultural, historical and political contexts.

Research, plan and make one independent production for a set brief in magazines, television, music video or online media.
Make the product for the intended audience named in the brief, within the stated lengths and amounts.
Write a Statement of Intent of about 250-300 words explaining how language, representation and audience targeting will be applied.
Use the forms of media language to communicate meaning, including denotation and connotation.
Choose elements of media language (selection, combination, exclusion) to shape meaning.
Use technology in relation to media language in the production.
Use codes and conventions that establish a style or genre.
Use links with other media products to influence meaning.
Re-present the world and construct a version of reality in the production.
Choose how to represent events, groups and ideas, using ideas of selection, construction and mediation.
Use or challenge stereotypes and understand how they let audiences read quickly.
Convey viewpoints, messages, values and beliefs, drawing on gender representation theory.
Aim the production at the specified audience, from specialised to mass.
Use technologies suited to reaching and being consumed by the audience.
Anticipate that audiences may interpret the product differently for social and individual reasons.
